pair_convention.spot_explanation: USD/JPY at 155.8121 means 1 USD buys 155.8121 JPY. A rising quote means USD strengthens and the yen weakens further; a falling quote means the yen strengthens and the dollar loses ground. All levels, targets and pip distances in this report are anchored to the payload spot of 155.8121 rather than the older 160.115/160.126 anchor both standalone dossiers used.

executive_summary: USD/JPY sits at 155.8121 as of the price payload's spotDate of 2026-09-03, meaning one dollar buys 155.81 yen, and the pair has fallen 1.24% over one month, 2.73% over three and 1.98% over six while remaining 6.37% higher over twelve — a twelve-month yen depreciation that has now given back most of its second-half gains in two sessions. The dominant bilateral narrative is no longer the one both dossiers were written around: the base dossier's headline claim that the Federal Reserve is the only G10 central bank expected to raise rates is void against this specific quote currency, because the Bank of Japan meets on 18 September, two days after the FOMC, with roughly 80% of a hike discounted and 50-75bp of consensus tightening still undelivered against a Fed whose own June dots make September terminal. That is the single most important differential the standalone views do not capture, and it is reinforced by a channel with no analogue anywhere else in the G10 — the US Treasury Secretary publicly lobbying the quote currency's central bank for a stronger yen. Against it stands a genuine and continuous pair-positive force: Japan's terms of trade have collapsed from 90.5 in Q1 2026 to 81.62 in July on an energy bill it must import while the base currency is a net energy exporter, and each further 100bp of BoJ tightening manufactures roughly JPY 5trn of Japanese debt service, which is the mechanism by which rising JGB yields have repeatedly failed to lift the yen. The settled verdict is tactically Neutral at conviction 2 (net score -0.074) and strategically Bearish at conviction 2 (net score -0.1086) — the pair falls over one to six months, with no directional edge over the next four weeks. The caveat, and it is a real one, is that the tactical Neutral was scored without sight of the price payload: spot now trades 482 pips below its 50-day, 418 below its 100-day and 265 below its 200-day average, has printed a lower high at 160.27 against July's 163.98, and delivered a 366-pip range on 3 September at 3.4 times ATR — in this analyst's reading the tactical evidence has moved to where the strategic score already sits, and a reader should treat the Neutral as the conservative end of a distribution that is now visibly skewed downward.

market_context.valuation_assessment: Pair-level valuation is extreme, stale as a timing tool, and worth stating only as a magnitude constraint. The BIS real effective rate for the yen was 65.3 in June 2026 — 30.4 points below the next-cheapest currency in the eleven-currency set and down 8.73 points on the year — while the dollar's was 107.84, the fourth highest. Mechanically scaling the current cross by that real gap implies a USD/JPY 'parity' near 96.95-96.73, explicitly labelled a real-exchange-rate relative rather than a PPP estimate. Neither has been a signal at any point in this cycle: the yen has been the cheapest major in the world for three years and got 8.73 points cheaper in the last one. What the level does do is bound the bear case, because it is the reason the US Treasury has repeatedly described the yen as substantially undervalued and the reason there is a publicly committed official bid in this pair and no official seller. Against a spot of 155.8121, a 54th-percentile closing position and a real effective rate at the floor of the floating era, the level of the pair is neither cheap nor rich against its own year and grotesquely cheap against its own decade.

market_context.recent_regime: The regime is one of failed official resistance to a carry trade that keeps re-forming, punctuated now by a repricing of the Japanese policy leg. Between 30 July and 26 August the Ministry of Finance bought JPY 15,399.3bn of yen including a joint operation with the US Treasury on 31 July, lifting the yen from just above 163 to 157, but by 1 September the pair had closed back at 160.19861. The 3 September session broke that pattern with a sharp yen surge of more than 2% to 155.28, attributed by BoJ accounts and market commentary to a re-calibration of rate-hike expectations rather than official intervention — a materially more durable event than the July episode and the single most important change in the pair's regime since both dossiers were written.

What has changed is the denominator: at 20-day realised volatility of 9.52% the carry-to-vol ratio has fallen roughly 20% from where it stood on 60-day data, and a further move to the 12-15% realised regime that accompanied the August 2024 unwind would take it to around 0.20 and make the position unattractive on a risk-adjusted basis without any change in rates at all. The roll, not the carry, is the real hurdle: the store's futures-implied premium of -291.3bp annualised implies roughly -29bp of yen cross-currency basis on top of the 262.5bp policy differential, meaning a rolled long-pair position must clear 291.3bp annualised, not 262.5bp, to remain profitable.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The bilateral differential is 262.5bp on policy (Fed 3.625% midpoint against a BoJ target 'at around 1.0 percent') and a payload 180bp on 10-year yields, though both 10-year legs are 2026-06-01 monthly vintages and the Japanese leg is the stale one: the live JGB 10-year printed 2.943% on 2026-08-31 and touched 3.00% on 2026-09-01, so the live long-end gap is nearer 175-180bp and has compressed roughly 11bp inside August entirely from the Japanese side. The single most important bilateral correction to the base dossier is that its headline claim — the Fed is the only G10 bank the market expects to raise rates — is void against this quote currency: the BoJ is expected to hike on 2026-09-18, two days after the FOMC, and is the bank with the longer distance still to travel. Pricing is asymmetric in a way that matters: roughly 80% of a BoJ move is discounted against roughly 57-66% of a Fed move, so the Fed decision carries the larger residual surprise, but the BoJ's PATH is the more under-priced object, with December OIS implying only about 1.21% against a MUFG path of 1.25% in September, 1.50% in January 2027 and 1.75% terminal, and Reuters sources describing a Board considering a faster cadence than twice a year. Transmission is direct and mechanical: USD/JPY is the highest-carry major and the pair reprices on the front-end differential, so a symmetric double hike leaves the differential unchanged while any BoJ acceleration language compresses it from the leg the market discounts most heavily.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the two policy paths diverge in the pair's favour on the downside, and this is the clearest dated argument available for USD/JPY falling. The Fed's own June projections put the funds rate at 3.8% for 2026 and 3.6% for 2027, which makes a September hike terminal on the Committee's own arithmetic, while the BoJ consensus has 1.50% by January 2027 and 1.75% thereafter — MUFG's published path is 1.25% in September, 1.50% in January and 1.75% in June 2027, and its US team's baseline has the Fed cutting. That takes the differential from 262.5bp toward roughly 225-235bp inside the window with the direction of travel unambiguous beyond it, and every decision that could deliver it is dated: FOMC 2026-10-28 and 2026-12-09 (SEP), BoJ 2026-10-30 (Outlook Report) and 2026-12-18. The balance-sheet channel points the same way: BoJ JGB purchases step down from JPY 2.5trn a month to JPY 2.1trn by Q1 2027 with interim assessments abolished, while the Fed has ended runoff and is buying bills, so the relative quantity settings are tightening in Japan and loosening in the US. The honest counterweight, and the reason confidence is 62 rather than higher, is that the differential was 180.0bp at the June vintage and 180.7bp at end-August on the 10-year while the pair rose 1.45% over six months — the rate channel has demonstrably been overwhelmed by the terms-of-trade and fiscal channels scored in Factors 5 and 8.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The growth differential is wide and favours the base currency: US GDP 2.1% year on year with an Atlanta Fed nowcast of 4.8% for Q3 and a composite PMI of 56.0, against Japanese GDP of 0.55% year on year and a Q2 print of just 0.3% quarter on quarter, 1.1% annualised, with private consumption contributing nothing for the first time in eight quarters. The inflation differential also favours the dollar in reaction-function terms rather than in real terms: US core PCE has been stuck at 3.3% for three months with headline at 3.7% and a six-month annualised rate of 4.1%, against Japanese core of 1.8% and a BoJ ex-special-factors measure of 2.3%. The bilateral point is that the US is above target and being forced to tighten while Japan is only now arriving at target, so the US price data has more capacity to surprise the less-priced of the two September decisions. Asymmetric sensitivity runs the same way: the 2026-09-04 payroll report and the 2026-09-11 CPI both land before the FOMC and both feed a decision priced at 57-66%, whereas Japan's 2026-09-17 CPI feeds one priced near 80%. The offset, and the reason confidence is only 52, is that the US labour data is deteriorating — payrolls -23,000 in July with 103,000 of prior downward revisions and average hourly earnings at a five-year low of 3.2% — so the tactical distribution has a fat left tail for the pair on 4 September.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the two sides of this factor genuinely offset for the pair. The US growth advantage is real and persistent — potential growth of roughly 2% against a Japanese potential of 0.5-1.0% — and that argues for the pair holding up. Against it, the inflation differential is set to converge from both ends: the US impulse is substantially a tariff level effect at an average statutory rate of 11.0% that drops out of year-on-year comparisons, while Japan's suppressed core is set to rise as government energy and education subsidies unwind, with the BoJ's own Outlook putting core CPI at 2.5% for FY2026 and revising FY2027 UP to 2.4%. Convergence of relative inflation with a widening US labour crack is the mechanism by which the policy differential in Factor 1 actually compresses, so scoring it directionally here as well would double-count the same evidence. The breadth of Japanese inflation remains narrow — a weighted median of 1.1% and services at 1.2% against goods at 2.7% — and there is a queued disinflationary impulse in rice, which is a real check on the convergence story. A Neutral scored on released statistics is the honest output where the growth differential and the inflation differential point in opposite directions with similar force.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: USD/JPY is a moderate-beta risk pair rather than a pure risk proxy, because both legs carry haven characteristics — but the asymmetry is that the yen is the funding leg of the global carry complex while the dollar is the invoicing and haven currency of first resort, so a benign risk regime is unambiguously pair-positive and only a genuine dislocation reverses it. The current regime is emphatically benign: VIX 14.43-14.51 after a 3.7 to 6.2 point collapse over the month depending on the observation date, US investment-grade OAS at 79bp and high yield at 260-263bp near post-crisis tights, the S&P 500 up 13.1% year to date and the Nikkei up 58.4% over twelve months. The Federal Reserve Chair has publicly said he would be hard pressed to describe broad financial conditions as restrictive, which means easy conditions are an argument for more tightening rather than a constraint on it — a doubly pair-positive configuration. The transmission is the carry trade itself: leveraged funds rebuilt 23,972 contracts of yen short over three consecutive weeks into exactly this environment. The live counterweight is geopolitical rather than financial — US and Iranian forces exchanged fire on 30-31 August in a severely disrupted Strait of Hormuz — and that is a tail rather than a state.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the modal path and the tail point in opposite directions with comparable expected value, which is what a Neutral is for. The modal path is persistence: if VIX stays near 14, credit stays at 79bp and equities compound, the pair grinds higher on carry exactly as it has for twelve months, and both dossiers independently reach a Neutral strategic risk stance. The tail is unusually well specified and is pair-negative: a Federal Reserve tightening into a labour market that shed 23,000 payrolls with 103,000 of downward revisions is the classic policy-error setup, the 2026-09-30 US appropriations deadline is live in a year that has already seen two federal shutdowns, US midterms fall on 2026-11-03, and the Hormuz situation has already escalated once. The yen's convexity to any of those is the highest in the G10 because the unwind mechanism is the carry trade itself, and both credit and equity vol are starting from levels that cannot compress further. Because the pair-negative tail is fat and the pair-positive modal path is more probable, and because six months gives the tail time to arrive, neither dominates.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months both legs' structural flow asymmetries point the same way for the pair, which is down. On the yen side, life-insurer currency hedge ratios are at historically low levels on both a Daiwa survey of ten majors and a Bank of Japan Review, and the trigger for normalisation is the base case itself: hedging costs fall as the BoJ hikes and the Fed peaks, and Daiwa states explicitly that raising ratios would prompt corresponding demand to purchase yen — spot demand invisible in any futures series. None of the ten insurers plans to increase unhedged foreign bonds and the median FY2026 term-end assumption is 154. On the dollar side, the base dossier's own strategic positioning stance is negative: a speculative long entering the window from a three-and-a-half-year high has far more room to be reduced than added, and the broad trade-weighted dollar fell 1.69% on the month against a G10 basket that fell 0.37%, which is the flow signature of structural dollar exposure being cut. The offset is real and it is why confidence is 55 rather than higher: the dollar's reserve share rose to 57.13% in Q1 2026 while the yen's fell 0.40pp to 5.44%, the largest single-quarter decline of any major currency, so official-sector allocation is working against the pair-bearish private-sector story.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: On levels Japan has the stronger external position — a current account surplus of 5.04% of GDP against a US deficit of 2.85-2.9% — but on trajectory the asymmetry runs the other way and hard. Japan's terms of trade have collapsed from 90.5 in Q1 2026 to 83.8 in Q2 and 81.62 in July, a 9.8% deterioration in two quarters, and the July trade balance widened 4.1-fold year on year to a deficit of JPY 638.3bn with mineral fuels at 22.1% of imports and up 53.5%, on falling volumes — price, not demand. June produced Japan's first monthly current-account deficit in seventeen months. The US, by contrast, is a net energy exporter, so the same energy prices that transfer Japanese national income abroad are a mild terms-of-trade positive for the base currency. Bilaterally, the IMF DOTS goods data cuts against the pair: the US ran a $68.5bn goods deficit with Japan in 2024, importing $148.2bn against $79.7bn of exports, which is a persistent structural yen-positive flow — but it is largely dollar-invoiced and slow-moving, and it has coexisted with an 8.59% pair appreciation over twelve months. Over four weeks the live inputs are the 2026-09-08 Japanese balance of payments and the 2026-09-15 trade statistics, both against a Brent price with Hormuz escalation live.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: At a 0.16 weight this is the heaviest counterweight to Factor 1, and the netting is genuinely close, which is why confidence sits at 50. Applying the framework's commodity direction rules bilaterally: oil up is mildly positive for the dollar (net energy exporter) and strongly negative for the yen (near-total import dependence), so the net effect of higher energy is the pair rising; LNG at a JKM price up 101.9% year on year is doubly yen-negative and roughly neutral-to-positive for the US. Against that, the composition of the US external position is deteriorating in a way that is new: the Q1 current account widened to 2.9% of GDP with the primary income balance flipping from surplus to deficit, which attacks the mechanism that has financed a minus $21.27trn net international investment position. Japan's surplus has the mirror-image composition problem — H1 primary income was 27.6 times the goods surplus, so the surplus is an investment-income stock return that does not generate spot yen demand, while the goods account that does is now in deficit. Add the $68.5bn bilateral goods deficit as a standing yen-positive and Japan's slide to third-largest net creditor with the net position falling to JPY 560.1trn, and the two sides very nearly cancel. The marginal edge goes to the pair rising because the energy transfer is continuous and monthly while the US income deterioration is quarterly and slow.

net_commodity_exposure.net_effect_calculation: Apply the framework rules leg by leg. Oil +10%: USD gets a mild positive (+) as a net exporter plus a hawkish inflation impulse; JPY gets a strong negative (−−) through a direct national-income transfer. Net: USD/JPY RISES — the quote currency is hurt more than the base is helped, and the base is helped rather than hurt. LNG (JKM) +10%: −− JPY, roughly neutral USD, so again the pair RISES. Gold +10%: mildly + CHF and, on current correlation, mildly + USD as a debasement hedge; no direct JPY channel. The netting is unambiguous in direction and the only question is magnitude, which the terms-of-trade series answers: Japan's index fell 9.8% in two quarters while the US ran a modest energy-export benefit, so the commodity channel is a persistent pair-positive. The one offsetting commodity-adjacent fact is that higher energy also lifts US inflation, which is the reason the Fed is hiking — so the channel is reinforcing rather than self-cancelling for this pair.
net_commodity_exposure.scenario_oil_up_10pct: Pair RISES. Japan's mineral fuel bill compounds from a July base of JPY 2,680.4bn and the terms-of-trade index heads below 78; the US gains mildly on exports and the Fed's inflation case hardens. Both legs push USD/JPY higher, and this is the specific channel through which Hormuz escalation is pair-positive.
net_commodity_exposure.scenario_oil_down_10pct: Pair FALLS, but less than symmetrically. Japan's terms of trade recover toward 86 and the current account stabilises, which is yen-positive; the US loses a mild export benefit but gains disinflation, which removes part of the Fed's tightening case — so the base leg's response is ambiguous and the net effect is a moderate pair decline.
net_commodity_exposure.dominant_commodity_driver: Crude oil, with LNG (JKM) a close second. Brent is the single variable that moves Japan's terms of trade, its monthly current account and the pair's strongest bearish-yen argument, and it is the variable a Hormuz escalation moves first.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Both central banks are guiding more hawkishly than their own curves, so the bilateral question is which gap is wider and which resolves first. The Fed's gap is measurable: the June dot median of 3.8% implies a 2026 hike outright while futures price 57-66%, and Warsh used Jackson Hole on 28 August to say better summer prints do not tell him underlying trends have improved. The BoJ's gap is larger relative to pricing beyond the next meeting: the 10 August Summary of Opinions contains the formulations that the pace of hikes will be faster than market expectations and that it is necessary to accelerate the pace, Takata dissented for 1.25% in July, Himino called on 27 August for raising rates in a timely manner and reiterated on 2 September that above-target inflation warrants more attention than in the past, and Ueda said on 1 September that the Board will debate a hike this month with upside price risks in mind and hopes to continue raising rates while conditions remain accommodative — against December OIS implying only about 1.21%. Two bilateral features have no analogue on the dollar side. First, sequence: the Fed reports on 16 September and the BoJ on 18 September, so the BoJ speaks last and gets to respond. Second, and unique to this pair, the US Treasury is publicly lobbying the quote currency's central bank: Secretary Bessent met Ueda at the G20 and called for decisive monetary steps to combat the weak yen. A base-currency government asking for a stronger quote currency is a pair-specific guidance fact that points one way.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the guidance divergence is directional rather than symmetric, and it is the second-heaviest pair-negative contributor. The BoJ has changed its stated objective — the July Outlook replaced lifting inflation toward 2% with stabilising it and preventing an upward deviation — which mechanically converts every upside surprise into a tightening impulse, and it abolished scheduled interim assessments of the JGB purchase plan, raising the probability of unscheduled hawkish action. The Fed's guidance, by contrast, is hawkish about a level it has already told the market is terminal: 3.8% for 2026 and 3.6% for 2027 means the next move after September is a cut, so dollar guidance decays with time while yen guidance compounds. Credibility runs the other way and is the offset: the FX market has been taught repeatedly this year that yen-positive news does not stick, so it discounts BoJ guidance, which is precisely why the gap to pricing is wide. The bilateral political overlay is unusual on both sides — Trump has said US rates are too high while exempting Warsh, and the US Treasury is asking Tokyo for a stronger yen — and both point the same way for the pair: political pressure makes a Fed hike a credibility demonstration rather than a sequence, and makes BoJ tightening the path of least resistance for both governments.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: The dominant pair-specific event risk is intervention, and intervention in USD/JPY is structurally one-directional: the Ministry of Finance buys yen, never sells it. Japan spent JPY 11,734.9bn in the 28 April-27 May window and JPY 15,399.3bn in the 30 July-26 August window, roughly JPY 27.1trn in 2026 against a previous full-year record of JPY 15.32trn, and the 31 July operation was conducted jointly with the US Treasury. Finance Minister Katayama said Japan will not hesitate to conduct further joint intervention and plans to use the Fed's FIMA repo facility; Secretary Bessent said Washington will not hesitate to participate again and repeated the point at the G20 on 31 August. There is a well-capitalised, publicly committed official bid in this pair and no corresponding official seller, which skews the tactical distribution downward regardless of the modal path — though the payload spot of 155.8121 sits well below the levels at which the July operations were conducted, so the immediate trigger is less proximate than it was a month ago. The second event set is the 16-18 September central bank cluster, a genuine 48-hour binary. Pointing the other way, the Hormuz escalation of 30-31 August is pair-positive through the energy channel scored in Factor 5, and the 2026-09-30 US appropriations deadline is pair-negative through the risk channel.

tactical.bilateral_analysis: Both sovereigns are deteriorating and both long ends are repricing simultaneously, so the pair-relevant question is which repricing is the more marginal and which inverts the normal FX transmission. Japan's does. Ministry budget requests for FY2027 submitted on 31 August total roughly JPY 143trn with a record debt-service line of JPY 36.6trn on an assumed rate lifted from 3.0% to 3.8%, and the market responded by taking the 10-year JGB to 3.00% on 1 September for the first time since 1996, the 2-year to a 31-year high of 1.743% and inverting 25s30s at -1.0bp — a supply-and-buyer-base signature, not a growth or policy signal. That matters for this pair specifically because it breaks the differential channel: rising JGB yields would ordinarily be yen-positive, and the fact that the pair did not fall as they rose is direct evidence that a meaningful share of the move is risk premium with no currency-positive content. The US side is worse in absolute size but better recognised and better rated: a deficit above $2trn, projected interest costs of $1,039bn, a 30-year at 5.22% and ratings of Aa1/AA+/AA+ against Japan's A1/A+/A, and the base dossier notes the tactical transmission is currently inverted there too, with the 1 September bond rout lifting yields and the dollar together. Two inverted transmissions on the same day, and Japan's is the one where the risk premium is newer.

strategic.bilateral_analysis: Over one to six months the interaction between Factor 1 and this factor is the most important thing in the dossier and it is asymmetric between the legs. Each further 100bp of BoJ tightening adds roughly JPY 5trn to Japan's debt-service line, about 0.9% of GDP annually, at the same time as the BoJ steps its JGB purchases down from JPY 2.5trn a month to JPY 2.1trn by Q1 2027 — supply rising as the dominant buyer withdraws, with the FY2027 draft budget approval in late December the specific decision point against the Prime Minister's stated JPY 40trn issuance cap. The US has the same interaction — a September hike raises the cost of rolling roughly $40trn of gross debt — but it starts from three rating notches higher, a debt stock roughly half the size relative to GDP on comparable measures, and a currency that is the world's reserve asset with a share that rose to 57.13% in Q1 2026 while the yen's fell to 5.44%. Japan's structural backstops are real and are why confidence is only 52: roughly 90% domestic ownership, the BoJ holding about half the outstanding stock, and three stable outlooks with no Big Three action in 2026. The net read is a modest pair-positive tilt: the fiscal channel is the mechanism by which yen strength keeps failing to stick.

catalysts.event: US August CPI and monthly federal budget balance
catalysts.rationale: The last US inflation print before the FOMC, against a July base of 3.4% headline and 2.5% core. The pair-relevant subtlety is that core CPI sits 80bp BELOW core PCE at 3.3%, an inversion of the normal sign, and the Fed targets PCE — so a soft core CPI is less dovish for the base leg than it looks, and the differential is more likely confirmed than compressed.

catalysts.event: FOMC decision, Summary of Economic Projections and press conference
catalysts.rationale: Roughly 57-66% priced for +25bp to 3.75-4.00%, so this is the less-discounted of the two September decisions and carries the larger residual surprise for the pair. It lands two days before the BoJ, which means it sets the tone the quote bank then responds to. The attached SEP also resets the strategic path: the 2027 median of 3.6% is what currently makes a September hike terminal.

July printed 1.9% headline and 1.8% core against a BoJ ex-special-factors measure of 2.3%, with government energy and education subsidies suppressing the official series by roughly 40-50bp. Tokyo core has accelerated three consecutive months and the 2025 rebasing lowered the year-ago base, so the arithmetic skews upward. A print at or above 2.0% the day before the BoJ makes the hike certain and pressures the cadence language.

catalysts.event: Bank of Japan Monetary Policy Meeting decision and press conference
catalysts.rationale: The largest pair event in the tactical window and, crucially, the last of the two — roughly 80% priced for +25bp to 1.25%, with Takata already dissenting for that level in July. The trade is not the decision but whether Ueda repeats the Summary of Opinions formulation that the pace will be faster than market expectations, which would move December OIS from roughly 1.21% toward a second hike and compress the differential from the leg the market discounts most. Market watchers attributed the 3 September yen surge to raised bets on a hike at this meeting after hawkish policymaker comments.

catalysts.event: US FY2027 appropriations deadline, US quarter-end dollar funding date and Japanese interim fiscal half-year close
catalysts.rationale: Three coincident events, two of them pair-negative. A US shutdown is precedented twice in 2026 and would be risk-negative, which is pair-negative through the yen haven channel; the Japanese interim book close generates documented repatriation and dividend flows that are pair-negative. Working the other way, this is the first quarter-end since reserves resumed falling to $2,916bn with the reverse repo facility drained to $702mn, and dollar funding pressure is pair-positive.

catalysts.event: FOMC decision (no Summary of Economic Projections)
catalysts.rationale: The first meeting after September with no dot plot attached, so the market must judge on the Committee's silence whether a September hike was terminal or the start of a sequence. Because the base leg's strategic contribution rests entirely on whether the June path of 3.8% then 3.6% holds, this is the identified inflection between our tactical Neutral and our strategic Bearish.

catalysts.event: Bank of Japan decision and quarterly Outlook Report
catalysts.rationale: The last clearly pair-negative scheduled event before the calendar turns hostile in November and December, and a projection round rather than a bare statement — which moves this pair materially harder. The July Outlook already revised FY2027 core CPI up to 2.4% and called price risks skewed to the upside; the October round incorporates a terms-of-trade shock and the subsidy unwind, and forecast revisions here are consistently under-anticipated. Morgan Stanley Research expects the BoJ at 1.25% in October and 1.5% in March.

Genuinely two-sided in the base leg — a result constraining fiscal expansion is dollar-positive through the deficit channel and negative through growth — and pair-relevant in a second way that is specific to this cross: the US Treasury's public appetite for supporting the yen has been linked to pre-midterm borrowing costs, so the election also marks the point after which the bilateral intervention commitment plausibly weakens. Analysis of the July operation argued US participation may have been designed to let Japan smooth its currency without creating more selling pressure on Treasury bonds.

catalysts.event: FOMC decision with Summary of Economic Projections
catalysts.rationale: The projection round that confirms or retires the hike-now-cut-later shape of the June dots. A 2027 median revised up removes the single largest component of our strategic Bearish reading and would be pair-positive; a confirmed 3.6% validates the compression thesis and is pair-negative. This is the base-leg counterpart to the BoJ's 18 December decision nine days later.

catalysts.event: Bank of Japan Monetary Policy Meeting decision
catalysts.rationale: The largest identified gap between guidance and pricing in the pair: December OIS implies roughly 1.21%, i.e. one 2026 hike and essentially nothing more, against a Board writing about acceleration, a MUFG path of 1.50% by January 2027 and 35 of 54 economists expecting at least 1.50% by end-March. Goldman noted 40 basis points of hikes priced into year-end, so a December move would be a repricing rather than a confirmation, and it compresses the differential from the discounted leg.

catalysts.event: Japan FY2027 draft budget Cabinet approval (dated to the fourth week of December on the FY2026 precedent of 26 December 2025 — not a gated date)
catalysts.rationale: The decision that determines whether the fiscal channel or the policy channel dominates the quote leg in 2027. Requests total roughly JPY 143trn with a record JPY 36.6trn debt-service line at a 3.8% assumed rate against a stated new-issuance cap of about JPY 40trn. A breach converts more of the JGB yield rise into sovereign risk premium, which is pair-positive precisely because it strips the currency-positive content out of higher Japanese yields.

assumptions: Price series quoted verbatim from the payload: the gated append-only store delivered dataPoints 130 bars over dateRange 2026-03-06 to 2026-09-03, with spot 155.8121 at spotDate 2026-09-03, pipSize 0.01 and a computationRange of 2007-11-22 to 2026-09-03 (4,900 weekday bars). weekendBarsDropped is 0, so every N-period window is a true trading-day window and all moving averages are simple averages of trading-day closes; the dataQuality note that only 2 resistance / 7 support zones met the 2-touch threshold has been supplemented with the 200-day/100-day averages and the 158.00/160.00 round numbers, labelled as such rather than presented as computed zones.

Spot date is two sessions ahead of the valuation date, not behind it: VALUATION_DATE is 2026-09-01 while spotDate is 2026-09-03, and the two intervening sessions contained a 439-pip decline. Every level, target, percentage and pip calculation in this report is anchored to 155.8121; both dossiers were written on a 160.115/160.126 anchor, so all their percentage figures — including the quote dossier's 8.59% twelve-month yen depreciation and its 1.45% six-month figure — differ from this report's payload-derived numbers (6.37% and -1.98% respectively), and the discrepancy is disclosed rather than reconciled.

Zone distances are measured to zone midpoints, which is how the payload computes distancePips and distancePct; where a lower or upper edge distance is more useful for level placement, it is stated separately and identified as such.

The option surface predates the spot anchor: impliedVol was observed 2026-08-31 with tenors of 38.6, 94.7 and 185.7 days, not calendar 1/3/6 months, because CME lists quarterly. Because the surface predates the 3 September session, all implied-versus-realised comparisons in this report understate the current gap. The quote dossier's separately sourced Saxo 1-month risk reversal of -1.74 volatility points differs from the store's -2.173 at 38.6 days; both are reported and the store governs.

The funding premium is not the policy differential: funding.premiumBp of -291.3 is the annualised premium between two listed futures (13.6-day and 48.6-day legs, observed 2026-08-31) and by covered interest parity is the interest differential plus the cross-currency basis, which cannot be decomposed without an OIS curve. The implied yen basis of roughly -29bp is a derivation, not a quote, and no quoted USD/JPY cross-currency basis was obtainable from any free source; all forward outrights are model forwards on an actual/365 basis, accurate to a few pips, not dealer quotes.

Both 10-year legs are stale monthly vintages: rates.base.yield10y of 4.47% and rates.quote.yield10y of 2.67% are both dated 2026-06-01 and the payload flags them explicitly as not live. The 180bp differential is therefore quoted only as a matched-vintage comparison; the live Japanese leg is materially higher (2.943% at 2026-08-31, 3.00% intraday on 2026-09-01), so every statement about long-end compression is sourced from the live figures and labelled accordingly.

Direction verdict carried verbatim: all ten factor blocks and the entire synthesis — stances, confidences, evidence types, applied weights, weighted contributions, net scores, score interpretations, conviction levels, overall confidences, rationales, G10 rankings, cross-horizon assessment and consensus-divergence assessment — are reproduced unchanged from the settled pass-1 verdict, which scored them without the price payload. Net stances were derived mechanically from the scores by the framework's threshold rule. Where this report disagrees with the settled tactical Neutral, it says so in prose without altering any stance, confidence or score.

Pass-1 source register (factor-level citation identifiers) references the direction verdict's own list, reproduced compactly to avoid collision with this report's Complete Citation List: D1 Reuters via Yahoo Finance; D2 Reuters via Investing.com; D3 The Japan Times; D4 MUFG Research; D5 Trading Economics; D6 FX BankForecast; D7 Bank of Japan Summary of Opinions/Statement; D8 Federal Reserve Board (Warsh); D9 Federal Reserve Board (FOMC Projections); D10 Ministry of Finance Japan (intervention operations); D11 CFTC (Traders in Financial Futures); D12 gated derived store; D13 IMF DOTS; D14 Japan Customs; D15 Bank of Japan Outlook; D16 the USD and JPY currency dossiers dated 2026-09-01.

Bilateral trade block used exactly as supplied — US exports to Japan $79.7bn, US imports from Japan $148.2bn, US net -$68.5bn, all 2024 annual goods — and not re-estimated from the web; it excludes services, in which the US runs a surplus with Japan, so the net goods figure overstates the total bilateral imbalance and is treated as a directional structural fact rather than a flow magnitude.

Consensus sourcing: the 23-desk figures and the second aggregate path are aggregators of bank research, not first-party desk publications, and their per-firm detail sits behind paid tiers. Morgan Stanley and Goldman Sachs figures are first-party. Individual targets attributed only through a third-party blog (ING 153, Scotiabank 150, a J.P. Morgan 164) are flagged as aggregator-reported and not relied on. Purely extrapolative forecast sites were excluded as a category error rather than treated as weak evidence.

Unexplained price action, now explained: the 3 September session was not attributable from the price payload alone; bilateral research resolved it as a policy repricing (BoJ accounts showed no sign of major intervention) rather than official flow, making the move more durable than the July intervention episode. Where the store's 155.30841 low and the vendor-reported 155.28 differ, the store governs.

No web-searched prices were used for spot, performance, moving averages, realised volatility, support/resistance levels, ATR or range percentiles; all such figures come from the gated store. Web research was used only for chart patterns requiring visual identification, pair-specific bank forecasts, positioning and flow commentary, bilateral investment flows, and the attribution of the 3 September session.
